title: Pesto Pasta Salad
subtitle: Fusilli in a basil, pine nut and Parmesan pesto with cherry tomatoes
excerpt: Short pasta tossed in a fresh basil pesto with cherry tomatoes and a handful of pine nuts. Served at room temperature as a lunch or picnic dish. The pesto goes further with a little pasta water stirred through.
sourceNotes: Pesto pasta salad became a British summer staple from the 1990s as supermarket pestos proliferated. The homemade version, based on the Genoese pesto formula of basil, pine nuts, Parmesan, garlic and olive oil (documented by Marcella Hazan and Elizabeth David among others), produces a pasta salad with noticeably more flavour. Served cold at a picnic or room-temperature for lunch, it is one of the most reliable things to make from a box of pasta.

recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. Make a large batch for picnics or meal prep.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best assembled on the day. The pesto will darken slightly on the surface; stir to refresh before serving.

content.text: Pesto pasta salad works because the pasta stays coated rather than drying out. The trick is to stir a couple of tablespoons of pasta cooking water through the pesto before tossing, which creates a slightly loose, silky emulsion that clings to every piece. Use short ridged pasta such as fusilli or penne; both hold pesto well.

items.prepNote: leaves only, plus extra to finish

content.text: Pound or blitz together {{basil}} of basil leaves, {{pine-nuts}} of toasted pine nuts, {{garlic}} of crushed garlic and {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt to a rough paste. Stir in {{parmesan}} of finely grated Parmesan and {{olive-oil}} of olive oil. Add {{black-pepper}} of pepper. The pesto should be thick and deeply green.

Cook {{pasta-dried}} of pasta in plenty of well-salted boiling water until just tender (al dente). Reserve 3 tablespoons of the pasta cooking water before draining. Drain the pasta in a colander, then tip into a large bowl.

Stir the reserved pasta water into the pesto, then pour over the warm pasta and toss to coat. Add the cherry tomatoes and toss again. Leave to cool to room temperature before serving, stirring once more to redistribute the pesto.

items.symptom: Pesto turns dark or dull on the pasta
items.cause: Basil oxidises when blended without enough oil, or when the pasta cools slowly while exposed to air.
items.fix: Coat the pasta immediately after draining while still hot. Lay a piece of clingfilm directly on the surface if making ahead.
Drizzle with another tablespoon of olive oil and toss. Add the extra pasta water gradually.

content.text: Pesto comes from Genoa, where the basil, pine nut and Parmesan sauce has been made since at least the 19th century. The cold pasta version is a British adaptation of the Italian warm original, made easy by supermarket pesto jars in the 1990s. It is now a picnic and lunch staple.
